..
Issued at 356 AM CDT Thu Oct 29 2026

Low-amplitude mid to upper level ridging is analyzed over the 
Northern Plains early this morning, with a surface ridge axis 
extending from southern Alberta to western North Dakota. A bank 
of low clouds across northern North Dakota has kept overnight 
temperatures in the 30s, while most locations to the south have 
fallen into the 20s. There is still potential for fog to develop
in southwest and south central North Dakota closer to sunrise 
this morning, but dewpoint depressions are already at or near 
zero with little to no wind, and some mid level clouds have 
developed. Little to no change is expected in the upper flow 
pattern today as the NW-SE oriented surface ridge axis slides 
eastward across the region. There are two potential areas for 
light precipitation this afternoon: one caused by low level 
warm air advection from far south central to southeast North 
Dakota and another from low level frontogenesis in far northwest
North Dakota. Measurable precipitation is not expected from 
either of them, and therefore is not being mentioned in other 
forecast products at this time. A quiet weather day is 
anticipated, with highs ranging from the lower and mid 40s north
to mid 50s southwest. The surface ridge axis is forecast to cut
through the northern Red River Valley tonight, leaving western 
and south central North Dakota under a light easterly flow. 
Forecast lows are mostly in the 20s, with a potential for low-
lying, sheltered areas to fall into the teens. High-resolution 
guidance shows two different potential fog regimes late tonight:
one from radiational cooling closer to the surface ridge in 
north central North Dakota, and another in the southwest driven 
by upslope flow with moisture advection.

The mid to upper level ridge is forecast to become more 
amplified over the region on Friday, but east to southeast low 
level/surface flow and a potential for a mostly cloudy sky 
could keep highs similar to today, with mid 40s north to lower 
and mid 50s south. From late Friday through Sunday, the 
mid/upper ridge axis should take on a negative tilt, turning 
flow aloft over the Northern Plains to the southwest. One to 
several shortwaves could eject from the base of a trough that 
moves over the western CONUS during that time period, placing 
low chances for light rain/drizzle in the local forecast at 
times. Temperatures are forecast to rise above normal this 
weekend, accompanied by unseasonably high dewpoints around 45 
to 55 degrees Fahrenheit. NBM projected high temperatures in 
the lower 50s to lower 60s on Saturday and mid 50s to mid 60s 
on Sunday may be a little too optimistic given expected cloud 
cover, but overnight lows should remain well above freezing. 

From late Sunday through Monday, the western CONUS trough is 
forecast to kick into the Plains, and could join forces with a 
northern stream shortwave diving down from Canada. Ensemble 
cluster analysis supports the medium to high chances for rain 
the NBM brings through the region Sunday night through Monday 
night, with all clusters showing high chances (greater than 70 
percent) for measurable rain over a 24-hour period. QPF 
threshold probabilities quickly lower for higher amounts, with 
only low chances for exceeding a quarter of an inch of rain. 
But the highest membership cluster (~35 percent) does have 
higher mean QPF and threshold probabilities than the other 3 
clusters. Temperatures are expected to remain above freezing 
throughout the event, keeping all precipitation as rain only. 
Sub-freezing temperatures do enter the forecast late Monday 
night, but that appears to be contingent on rain and associated
cloud cover departing sooner. In other words, if precipitation 
lingers Monday night into Tuesday, which is supported by ~55 
percent of the total ensemble membership, Monday night/Tuesday 
morning temperatures are more likely to remain above freezing. 
Forecast uncertainty approaching the middle of next week is 
rooted in the eastward progression of the central CONUS trough, 
but all solutions would leave the Northern Plains under a 
northwest flow pattern. The lowest-membership cluster on 
Wednesday drives a potent trough into the Upper Midwest, but 
other clusters tend to keep this feature weaker and/or further 
north. Spread in the NBM temperature distribution grows by the 
middle of next week, but the 25th percentile keeps both highs 
and lows near average (mid 40s and mid 20s, respectively), with 
the 75th percentile of each around 10 degrees above average.
